epc-glasgow.prose:
Homes in Glasgow

Glasgow's housing is dominated by flats. Red and blond sandstone tenements fill the West End, Partick, Dennistoun, Shawlands and Strathbungo, alongside interwar and post-war homes in the outer neighbourhoods and newer flats along the Clyde. Each brings its own EPC issues:

  • Sandstone tenements have thick solid walls with no cavity to fill, so the rating depends heavily on the heating, the windows and whether the flat is on a middle floor, the top floor or the ground floor.
  • Top-floor flats lose heat through the roof. If there is a loft above, insulation there can make a real difference, but it is often shared, so evidence of any work matters.
  • Flats with electric heating, common in 1960s and 1970s blocks and some conversions, often rate E or lower. High heat retention storage heaters are the usual recommendation.
  • Newer flats and houses built since around 2010 usually rate B or C.

We are based at 272 Bath Street in the city centre, so most Glasgow appointments are close by. We regularly work for landlords and letting agents in the West End, Southside, Merchant City and Finnieston, where the EPC and the legionella risk assessment are often booked together.

epc-edinburgh.prose:
Homes in Edinburgh

Much of Edinburgh's housing is older and protected, which shapes both the rating and what can be done about it:

  • Georgian and Victorian tenements in the New Town, Stockbridge, Marchmont and Bruntsfield have solid stone walls, large sash windows and high ceilings. They often rate D or E.
  • Listed buildings and conservation areas cover large parts of the city. In Scotland they still need an EPC when sold or let, but changes such as replacement windows or external insulation need consent, so secondary glazing and draught-proofing are often the practical options.
  • Leith and the waterfront mix older tenements with modern flats that usually rate B or C.
  • Suburban houses in areas like Corstorphine, Liberton and the south of the city are typically interwar or post-war, where loft and cavity insulation are the main recommendations.

Edinburgh has a large private rented sector, student lets and HMOs. Short-term let hosts must meet the Repairing Standard too, which includes the duty to assess legionella risk. We can do the EPC and the legionella risk assessment in one visit for £120 + VAT.

epc-bearsden.prose:
Homes in Bearsden

Bearsden is mostly houses rather than flats, and many are larger or older than average:

  • Victorian and Edwardian villas with solid stone walls, bay windows and rooms in the roof. Extensions built at different times are common, so the assessor records each part separately.
  • Interwar bungalows and semis, often with cavity walls. Filled cavities and good loft insulation usually lift these to C or D.
  • Post-war and newer detached houses, where the boiler and heating controls make the biggest difference.

Larger homes with several extensions take a little longer to survey. Having the dates of extensions and any insulation paperwork to hand helps the rating reflect the work you have done.

Homes in Bishopbriggs

Bishopbriggs grew quickly from the 1930s onwards, so most homes are semis, bungalows and terraces from the middle of the twentieth century, with newer estates on the edges:

  • 1930s to 1970s semis and bungalows usually have cavity walls. Whether the cavity has been filled, and how thick the loft insulation is, decide a lot of the rating.
  • Newer estates built since the 1990s are often timber frame with insulation built in, and usually rate C or better.
  • Flats around the town centre and Kirkintilloch, where the heating system is the main factor.

If you have had cavity wall insulation installed, a guarantee from the installer is the best evidence, because the assessor cannot always confirm it by looking at the outside of the wall.

  • Newer private estates on the edges of town, usually rating B or C.

legionella-risk-assessment-glasgow.title: Legionella Risk Assessment Glasgow | From £65 | Scotland EPC
legionella-risk-assessment-glasgow.desc: Legionella risk assessments for Glasgow landlords, letting agents and short-term let hosts. From £65 per property, or £120 with an EPC, plus VAT. Written assessment with temperatures and actions.
legionella-risk-assessment-glasgow.lede: Legionella risk assessments for rented flats and houses across every Glasgow postcode. From £65 per property, or £120 with an EPC at the same visit, plus VAT.
legionella-risk-assessment-glasgow.prose:
Glasgow water systems

Most Glasgow rented flats have one of two systems, and the risk is quite different:

  • Combi boilers heat water on demand with nothing stored, so they are usually low risk. We still check outlet temperatures, showers and any little-used taps.
  • Hot water cylinders, often with an electric immersion heater in older tenements and 1960s to 1970s flats. Here we check the cylinder reaches 60°C and the hot water at the taps reaches 50°C. Top-floor flats sometimes have a cold water tank in the loft above.

Houses in the suburbs are more likely to have a loft tank and cylinder, which is where we most often find a missing lid, debris or warm cold water.

Empty flats and student lets

Water that sits still is the biggest risk. Flats that stand empty between tenancies, and student lets over the summer, should have every outlet flushed before the next tenant moves in. We include this in the action list if it applies.

What we check

We identify the water system, measure temperatures at the taps, cylinder and any tank, inspect tanks for lids and debris, and look for showers, dead legs and little-used outlets. You get a written assessment with the temperatures recorded, an overall risk level and a short list of actions. More about legionella risk assessments.

The rules in Scotland

The Repairing Standard guidance says a private landlord must have the water system assessed for legionella before the property is first let, and review it at intervals of no more than two years. There is no legionella certificate and water testing is not normally needed.

Short-term lets and HMOs

Edinburgh has a large number of short-term lets and HMOs. Short-term let hosts must meet the Repairing Standard, which includes the duty to assess legionella risk. Properties that sit empty between guests are a particular risk, because water stagnates in the pipes and shower hoses.

HMOs and larger flats often have shared tanks or long pipe runs. We will quote for these once we know the size of the system.

Older tenements

New Town and Marchmont flats often have cylinders in cupboards and, on top floors, tanks in the roof space. Old pipework that once fed a removed bathroom or kitchen can leave dead legs, which the Repairing Standard guidance says should be removed.

What we check

We identify the water system, measure temperatures at the taps, cylinder and any tank, inspect tanks for lids and debris, and look for showers, dead legs and little-used outlets. You get a written assessment with the temperatures recorded, an overall risk level and a short list of actions. More about legionella risk assessments.

Yes. Short-term lets must meet the Repairing Standard, which includes assessing legionella risk before letting and reviewing it at least every two years.
